summary: Defines version 2 of the Service Location Protocol, a framework that lets computers discover network services such as printers with little or no manual configuration. It is designed to scale from small networks to larger ones.

plainLanguage.summary: Service Location Protocol version 2 (SLPv2) helps an application find a service such as a printer without knowing the computer that provides it. It searches by service type and details, and can use a directory to collect service listings.

questions: how do hosts discover printers automatically
what is a directory agent in slp
subtitle: A protocol for finding network services by type and features instead of host name.

tldr.problem: Applications often need a service's host name before they can use it, which requires manual configuration. SLP lets a user or program search for services by type and attributes.
tldr.mechanism: Service Agents advertise services, User Agents request matching services, and optional Directory Agents collect advertisements and answer requests. Scopes limit which services an agent can see.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2608 updates SLPv1 in RFC 2165 and is itself updated by RFC 3224. It is intended for networks under cooperative administrative control, not global wide-area discovery.

today: RFC 2608 is a Proposed Standard that updates SLPv1 in RFC 2165 and has been updated by RFC 3224. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Finding Services by Description
sections.content:
The Service Location Protocol (SLP) gives hosts information about the existence, location, and configuration of network services. Instead of supplying a host name, a user supplies a service type and attributes that describe the service; SLP returns its location.

RFC 2608 updates SLP version 1 (RFC 2165), correcting protocol errors, adding features, and removing some requirements. It is designed for networks under cooperative administrative control, such as enterprise networks with shared services. The RFC warns that it may not scale to discovery across the global Internet or to very large networks.
sections.plainLanguage: A program can search for a kind of service and describe what it needs, without knowing the service computer's name. SLP is designed for a managed network, where administrators can organize services and users.

sections.title: User, Service, and Directory Agents
sections.content:
A User Agent (UA) searches for services on behalf of a user. A Service Agent (SA) advertises services. A Directory Agent (DA) collects those advertisements and acts as a cache.

Without a DA, a UA multicasts a Service Request and matching SAs reply directly. With a DA, SAs register services and the UA sends a unicast request to the directory. Registrations expire unless refreshed. Agents discover DAs through requests and advertisements, or can use configured addresses.

SLPv2 agents do not directly hear replies from SLPv1 agents. The RFC recommends that SLPv2 implementations support SLPv1; a DA supporting both versions can allow agents using the two versions to interoperate.
sections.plainLanguage: A service agent announces what it offers, and a user agent asks for what it needs. A directory agent can collect announcements so users can search one place instead of contacting every service.

sections.title: Service Types, URLs, and Attributes
sections.content:
A service location is expressed as a URL. A service type can be based on the URL scheme or use the service: scheme. An abstract type such as service:printer can match concrete types such as printer services using LPR or HTTP.

A Naming Authority defines the meaning of service types and attributes; IANA is implied when no authority is named. Attributes describe a service and may be integers, strings, Boolean values, or opaque byte sequences. A request can include a predicate to select services by attribute values.

Scopes group services, usually for administrative purposes. An agent searches only the scopes it is configured to use. The default scope string is DEFAULT, and scope strings are case-insensitive.
sections.plainLanguage: A service listing gives its location, its type, and details such as attributes. A search can ask for a type of service and filter results by those details.

sections.title: Messages and Matching Replies
sections.content:
Every SLP message begins with a header that gives the version, Function-ID, message length, flags, extension offset, transaction identifier (XID), and language tag. Strings use UTF-8, are not null-terminated, and have a two-byte length before them. Replies copy the XID from the request; a retransmitted request keeps the same XID.

The required messages include Service Request, Service Reply, Service Registration, Service Acknowledgment, and Directory Agent Advertisement. Other messages support functions such as asking for attributes or browsing service types. Errors are returned only for unicast requests; a multicast request that would cause an error is silently discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: The header identifies the message type and the request it belongs to. A reply copies the request's transaction identifier so the requester can match the answer.

sections.title: Transport, Registration, and Retries
sections.content:
SLP uses UDP port 427. Requests use multicast by default, and broadcasts can substitute on isolated networks. The default maximum SLP message size in a UDP datagram is 1400 bytes, excluding UDP and other headers. A message that does not fit is truncated with the OVERFLOW flag; a User Agent may retry over TCP. Large service registrations and deregistrations must use TCP.

An SA registers a service with its URL, lifetime, type, scopes, and attributes. A fresh registration replaces the prior one. An incremental registration updates only the attributes it supplies, and MUST NOT be used for services registered with authentication blocks. Registrations expire unless refreshed.

Requests with no response are retransmitted after exponentially increasing waits. Multicast requests include a Previous Responder List so agents that already replied can remain silent.
sections.plainLanguage: Service agents register their listings with a directory, and refresh them before they expire. If a request gets no reply, SLP retries it and waits longer between attempts.

sections.title: Optional Authentication Blocks
sections.content:
Authentication blocks can let an agent check that service URLs, attributes, and advertisements were not changed and came from an authorized agent. A block includes a timestamp, an SLP Security Parameters Index (SPI), and signature information. The SPI identifies keying material and parameters needed for verification.

All SLP agents MUST implement DSA with SHA-1, identified by BSD 0x0002. Agents must be configured with the information needed to produce or verify signatures. A DA expects later updates or removals to include authentication blocks for SPIs used in the original registration.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature can help a receiver check who supplied a service listing and whether it changed. The agents need keys and settings configured in advance to verify it.

sections.title: Security Limits
sections.content:
SLP can authenticate service URLs and attributes, but it does not provide confidentiality. The RFC says sites that need confidentiality should protect SLP messages with IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP).

Without signature generation and verification, an attacker could advertise a service on a server it controls or carry out selective denial-of-service attacks. The RFC advises sites in hostile environments to consider distributing keys before deploying sensitive agents. Without prior configuration, the described authentication mechanisms cannot be used.
sections.plainLanguage: SLP signatures can help detect fake or changed service listings, but they do not hide message contents. The signature system needs keys configured before agents use it.
